title: Thermal and Power-Induced Performance Drift Across Cloud SKUs (A100 / H100 / L40S)
content:
Summary:

This doc records an exploratory bench focused on how sustained power draw and thermal behavior across cloud GPU SKUs (A100, H100, L40S) impact runtime performance for long-context generation workloads. The goal is to surface non-obvious performance drift modes (throughput drop, latency jitter, tail amplification) correlated with thermal/power events and driver/CUDA combinations, and to produce pragmatic mitigations for the serving runtime and deployment configs.

Why we ran this:
- We keep seeing occasional throughput drops after ~30–90 minutes on long-running generation tests in Dedicated clusters; root cause has been fuzzy.
- Existing SKU comparisons looked at raw latency and occupancy but not sustained thermal drift under realistic long-context workloads.
- Ops reported a few incidents where different host types with identical instance sizes behaved differently after sustained load.

Hypotheses:
1) Sustained high-utilization long-context workloads cause subtle thermal/power management behaviors (clock throttling, power capping) that reduce sustained throughput even when initial microbenchmarks look fine.
2) Different driver / CUDA combinations expose different firmware-level power-management heuristics, so behavior will vary across driver versions even for the same SKU.
3) L40S (with larger thermal headroom in our runs) will show less drift than older A100 configs; H100 may be sensitive to local power/BIOS settings and show more frequent short-term throttling.

Test matrix (summary):
- GPUs: NVIDIA A100 (40GB), NVIDIA H100 (80GB), NVIDIA L40S (48GB)
- Cloud SKUs (representative): AWS p4d.24xlarge (A100), AWS p5.48xlarge (H100), Azure NV-L40s_v3 (L40S), GCP a2-highgpu variants (A100)
- Driver / CUDA combos: 
  - Nvidia driver 525.105 + CUDA 11.8
  - Nvidia driver 535.86 + CUDA 12.1
  - Nvidia driver 555.xx (preview) + CUDA 12.2 (on H100 tests)
- Workloads: sustained autoregressive generation with 8k and 32k context lengths, token-by-token streaming (no aggressive batching), 1 and 4 concurrent streams per GPU, prompt prefixes warmed, 10-minute warmup then 120-minute steady window.
- Metrics collected: per-token latency, p50/p95/p99, throughput (tokens/s), GPU power (W) sampled via DCGM @1s, GPU clock (sm, mem), temperature (C), GPU utilization, NVML event logs, and system-level CPU+I/O counters.

Methodology notes:
- We pinned exclusive GPU allocation (no multi-container interference).
- Tests run inside the same image + runtime binary across SKUs; only kernel driver / CUDA stack swapped where tested.
- For each SKU/driver combo we repeated the 120-minute steady test 3x on different hosts and averaged.
- Telemetry synchronized to a common timebase to allow cross-correlation of power spikes and latency spikes.
- Logging retained for post-mortem (NVML logs + DCGM snapshots every 1s).

Key results (high-level):
- Drift pattern: On A100 SKUs (p4d and GCP a2 variants) we observed a modest 5–12% throughput drop (tokens/s) over the 120-minute window under 32k context + 4 streams. The throughput decline correlated tightly with stepwise decreases in sustained SM clock and occasional short power-capping events (~2–6s). Temperature rose steadily to ~86–89C before clock steps.
- H100 behavior: H100 runs showed more abrupt tail-latency amplifications at ~25–50 minute marks. These correlated with driver/firmware transitions where power/clock governors toggled to a more conservative profile. The degree of degradation was driver-dependent: driver 535.xx + CUDA12.1 saw ~18% sustained throughput reduction and p99 spikes >2.5× baseline, while newer 555.xx drivers (preview) showed smaller sustained drops but more frequent short spikes.
- L40S behavior: L40S SKUs were the most stable in our test matrix. Sustained throughput variance stayed within ±3% and tail latencies were stable. Peak temperatures ran ~5–7C lower for comparable workloads; power draw was slightly lower but less variable.
- Driver impact: Across all SKUs, moving from driver 525 -> 535 reduced some short-term jitter but in a few H100 configurations introduced a new conservative governor path that increased p99 latency. Drivers matter as much as base SKU in observed drift modes.

Representative data points (single-run extracts):
- A100 (p4d) driver 525/CUDA11.8 — initial 1200 tokens/s, drifted to 1075 tokens/s over 120min (~10.4% drop). SM clocks: 1410MHz -> stepped to 1305MHz at t≈42min. Temperature 72C -> 88C.
- H100 (p5-like host) driver 535/CUDA12.1 — initial 1600 tokens/s, sustained 1310 tokens/s after abrupt drop at t≈37min (~18.1% drop). p99 increased from 480ms to 1320ms during spike windows.
- L40S (azure) driver 535/CUDA12.1 — initial 1400 tokens/s, ±2% fluctuation only, temperature plateau ~81C, no SM clock stepping observed.

What we saw in the logs (correlation examples):
- NVML showed repeated short power cap events on A100 hosts immediately preceding clock-step events. The power cap messages matched the approximate time windows where tokens/s dropped.
- H100 NVML traces included entries where the firmware transitioned to a lower performance profile after a cumulative energy threshold was hit (vendor-specific telemetry). These transitions corresponded to elevated p99s.

Interpretation / hypotheses refined:
- Sustained long-context generation stresses sustained power delivery and thermal systems in ways microbenchmarks don't trigger. Even without hitting a hard thermal throttling ceiling, vendor firmware can apply conservative clock adjustments or power caps to preserve hardware longevity or meet data-center power budgets; these have measurable impact on sustained throughput and tail latency.
- L40S hardware/board design appears less prone to this particular protective behavior in our sample hosts (likely higher thermal headroom and different voltage/frequency scaling curve).
- Driver/firmware combinations significantly influence when and how those protections engage; a later driver may include safety updates that trade some sustained performance for predictability or reliability.

Immediate recommendations for serving runtime and infra teams:
1) Avoid long single-stream ultra-long context single-GPU placements for latency-sensitive routes without testing sustained 1–2 hour windows on the target SKU + driver combo. If customers require 32k+ and p99 SLAs, prefer SKUs that showed stability (L40S-like) or dedicate thermal/power headroom.
2) Add a sustained-run gating test to our CI canary for Dedicated images: 30–60m steady long-context run focused on detecting SM-clock steps / power-capping behavior. Fail the canary if sustained throughput drops >10% or p99 > threshold.
3) Expose a deployment-facing capability to pin driver version per node-pool or signal a recommended driver matrix in the Console per SKU. Make driver matrix part of the Dedicated onboarding checklist.
4) Runtime-level mitigation: implement proactive small-scale inter-request pacing (micro-sleep between large context requests) or adaptive concurrency reduction under detected trend of rising temperature/power draw to avoid stepping into firmware-protected regimes that produce abrupt tail spikes.
5) For enterprise customers with strict SLAs, recommend Dedicated nodes with enforced thermal headroom (lower GPU packing / reserved headroom) or L40S class nodes where available. Document cost-throughput tradeoff.

Open questions / follow-ups:
- How consistent is this across AZs/hosts? We saw host-to-host variability in the A100 pool; need larger N tests across cloud regions.
- Can BIOS or host power profile knobs (OEM settings) shift the thresholds? Need vendor engagement with cloud providers to understand host-level power governors.
- Is there a way to detect imminent firmware-driven profile changes earlier via DCGM heuristics so we can gracefully reduce concurrency before tail spikes?

Next steps (action items):
- [Short] Add a 60m long-context sustained run to the Dedicated canary (owner: Samir) — JIRA-ENG-1274.
- [Med] Run expanded N=10 host sweep across multiple zones for A100 and H100 to measure host-to-host variance (owner: Miguel).
- [Med] Add an experimental telemetry detector in the runtime to correlate 1s DCGM power jumps with rising p99 and test adaptive concurrency fallback (owner: Ellen).
- [Long] Open provider support tickets with AWS/Azure/GCP quoting NVML traces and ask for host-level power/BIOS translucency (owner: Asha).

Appendix: quick troubleshooting checklist for ops when an application reports slow drift
- Capture 120s NVML/DCGM trace from affected host. Check for power cap events and SM clock changes.
- Compare driver versions against our stable matrix in Console. If host is on a conservative driver, flag for driver rollback test in staging.
- If sustained thermal trend exists, consider shifting workloads to other nodes or temporarily reducing concurrency until cooled.

Notes and caveats:
- This was an exploratory internal bench with limited host samples (N≈3 per config). Results are directional and intended to drive follow-ups, not to be used as a final vendor scorecard.
- Power/thermal behavior can be influenced by host OEM configs and datacenter environmental conditions (ambient temperature, rack airflow); we did not control those variables beyond sampling multiple hosts when available.

If you want the raw CSV/DCGM logs or a quick plotting notebook, see linked artifacts (github PR includes the analysis notebook and scripts).

-- Asha
